extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American government; civic reformers and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess defects in the composition and conduct of U.S. state legislatures and the institutional remedies proposed (e.g., bicameralism, veto, commissions, separation of private bills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferiority of legislators (knowledge, skill, conscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferiority, as respects knowledge, skill, and sometimes also conscience, of the bulk of the men who fill these bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a core defect: many members are ignorant, narrow, or lacking statesmanlike knowledge; composition varies by region (New England better, large cities worse). Consequences include inability to grapple with difficult questions, susceptibility to manipulation by schemers, and enactment of ill-considered laws. Examples: farmers, small lawyers, or inexperienced city representatives who are corruptible or simply ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvidence in matters of finance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures incur large and unnecessary state and local indebtedness and waste public funds. Evidence cited includes the enormous number of statutes and the estimated public expense of legislative sessions (estimates of cost per diem and total outlay). Remedy discussion ties to veto powers and better control by public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heedlessness in passing administrative bills
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators pass administrative or technical measures without understanding consequences; sometimes executive commissions or judges must report and propose reforms because legislatures lack capacity. This leads to poor administrative law and requires quasi-judicial or expert-led solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of proper methods for dealing with local and special bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Want of proper methods for dealing with local and special bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large share of legislative time is spent on private/local acts (incorporations, name changes, releases from indebtedness), which consumes resources and fosters jobs. The author recommends separating private/local bills from general legislation and handling them by general principles or quasi-judicial methods (e.g., Public Utilities Commission experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of public opinion adequately to control legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of public opinion adequately to control legislation, and particularly local and special bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public opinion is weak or ill-informed, private interests capture legislation. The text notes the improving but still inadequate role of public opinion, the value of referendum in some States, and the importance of vigilant citizens and reformers in checking abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of corruption (bribery, black-mailing, lobby influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corrupt member has several methods of making gains: exact money for his vote; black-mailing by introducing threatening bills; the lobby soliciting members with inducements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed examples: money for votes, blackmail via bills 'kept in the paper till the last moment', constant presence of corporate agents during sessions, treating members to dinners/drinks/cigars, and difficulty of convicting known corrupt men. Remedies discussed: committee scrutiny, public opinion, veto, and institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Log-rolling and vote-trading as a corrosive practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Log-rolling: securing support for a measure by trading support on other measures, often to benefit particular local interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from legitimate give-and-take; in its mischievous forms several Constitutions expressly treat it as solicitation or bribery. Log-rolling arises from localism and the rule that a member is sole exponent of his district; it is hard to police and underlies many 'jobs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee power and chairmanship as focal corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairmanship of a committee the position which affords the greatest facilities for an unscrupulous man; committees are the focus of intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees can smuggle jobs through; control of committee processes and chairmanships concentrates power and creates opportunities for lobbyists and corrupt agents to exert influence. Vigilant oversight and transparent committee procedures are implied remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism: members put district first, impairing state interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of localism completely rules them. A member is... bound to think first of the general welfare of his constituency (Brownsville, Pompey, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localism makes members judge measures by local effect only, discourages interference by others, and normalizes log-rolling. It reduces the number of 'members for the State' and results in many needless or bad bills that harm general welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, episodic sessions and restlessness leading to rushed legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting for only a few weeks in the year, or probably in two years, they are alarmingly active during those weeks, and run measures through whose results are not apprehended till months afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sessions create haste and poor deliberation; many bills are introduced but few pass because of time or committee pressure. Author cites large annual outputs of statutes and recommends institutional reforms (commissions, longer/structured deliberation) to mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and composition of Senate vs House affects corruption susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In demoralized States the State Senate is apt to be a worse body than the House... As the Senate is smaller... the vote of each member is of more consequence, and fetches, when venal, a higher price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller chambers make individual votes more valuable and attract practiced intriguers; the Senate's confirmation powers increase temptation. Evaluators should compare chamber size, power, and selection dynamics when assessing vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timidity and lack of legislative independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more remarkable about these State legislators than their timidity. No one seems to think of having an opinion of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators often follow party, constituents, or current outcries rather than exercise independent judgment. While this can allow zealous minorities to enact reforms, it more often results in unprincipled or opportunistic lawmaking; cultivating independent leadership and responsible officeholders is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume and character of legislation (many local/special acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual output of all the legislatures has been estimated at 15,000 statutes... The large majority of these were local or special, intended to further the interests of particular persons or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High volume, primarily local/special acts, indicates misallocation of legislative time and expense, and is a marker of jobbery. Statistical measures (counts of statutes, proportion local vs general) are useful evaluative metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into two houses as a check on bad legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: First, there is the division of the legislature into two houses. A job may have been smuggled through one house, but the money needed to push it through the other may be wanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bicameral disagreement is viewed as salutary because many new measures are more likely to harm than help; two chambers provide opportunity to expose tricks and stop bad bills. Use as an institutional safeguard when assessing legislative design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power of governor (including item veto) as a defensive mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, there is the veto of the governor... some constitutions... provide that the governor may reject one or more items of an appropriation bill... and this has been found to strengthen his hands immensely in checking the waste of public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The governor's veto concentrates responsibility and compels executive scrutiny of bills; the item veto is particularly effective against appropriations abuses. Evaluations should consider the scope and use of veto powers in a State's checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of administrative officers/boards and quasi-judicial commissions as remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The recent creation of various administrative officers or Boards has gone some way to meet the difficulties... The Public Utilities Commission charged with dealing with agencies of transportation and other public services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissions can prepare technical bills, provide systematic treatment of sectors, and reduce fragmentary legislative action. The author cites New York's Public Utilities Commission as an experiment with promise; separation of private legislation to quasi-judicial bodies is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vest appointment power in the governor (appointments versus direct election)
rubrics_metrics.description: They might, in the opinion of some judicious publicists, be improved by vesting the appointment of the chief officials in the governor, instead of leaving it to direct popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizing appointments in the executive can produce more unity of purpose and administration; discussed as a possible improvement to executive arrangements to counter fragmented, elected officeholders whose competing ambitions weaken coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of vigilant reformers and public-spirited minorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A few energetic reformers went to Albany and Harrisburg to strengthen the hands of the little knot of members who battle for good government... and partly frightened, partly coaxed a majority... into adopting proposals opposed to the interests of professional politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of determined reformers, philanthropic citizens, and active newspapers can overcome entrenched jobbery and produce salutary reforms (secret ballot, civil service improvement). This is an important non-institutional corrective to evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and regional composition as indicators of legislative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The best seem to be those of some of the New England States... The lowest place belongs to the States which, possessing the largest cities, have received the largest influx of European immigrants... New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Chicago... have done their best to poison the legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legislative quality by region, urbanization, and social composition: traditions, landed farmers, and older commonwealths often sustain better tone; large cities with recent immigrant influxes and concentrated capital are more prone to bossism and corruption.
